title: 观点：在游戏开发中优先“核心团队”时，措辞为何重要
content:
Why overly praising 'core teams' may devalue developers
Production
Business
Commentary
Opinion: Why words matter when we prioritize 'core teams' in game development
How we describe game development will inevitably shape our processes.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
October 22, 2026
schedule
6 Min Read
Image via Fuse Games/Secret Mode
A recent social media dustup in the game development community has given the industry reason to scrutinize the phrase "core team." Said dustup occurred after Gamesindustry.biz
published an in-depth story
breaking down the "distributed development" model that Fuse Games
employed
in the making of
Star Wars: Galactic Racer
. Said model divides the development team into three categories centered around a "core team."
It's a useful framework for describing a complex method for creating games that require hundreds of developers to bring across the finish line—so why did a number of developers
express frustration
over a Bluesky post from the outlet (disclaimer—
I was among those
voicing such a reaction) that stated "Star Wars: Galactic Racer was made by a core team of 75 people"?
It's a valid question—one that takes on more weight when you realize how many studios are establishing development practices similar to Fuse's distributed development model. The answer comes down to how you interpret the phrase "was made by," as a similar sentence appears in the story itself.
Related:
Fuse Games CEO breaks down codev framework for Star Wars: Galactic Racer
The statement is factually true as Fuse Games' core team often consisted of fewer than 75 people during development. But is is also
not
true, as the game was truly made by roughly 1,100 people who appear in the game's credits. One could interpret the phrase as a neutral descriptor of the "core team"—but one could also interpret it as obscuring the work of the hundreds of developers who helped bring us the viral delight that is
Biddy Blas
.
It's intended to be the former. GI.biz features editor Lewis Packwood confirmed as much to me in an email exchange this week, where he pointed out the phrase "core" is a word Webster used to refer to the team at Fuse Games. "Both his comments and the article made clear that Galactic Racer was the work of many different people in different places, not just the 75 staff at Fuse Games," he explained. "Given that this model of a small full-time team directing and coordinating a range of external companies is relatively new to the games industry, it may just be that we haven't yet developed the proper language to adequately describe it."
Packwood (who deserves a tip of the cap for participating in this inadvertent exercise in public editing) has absolutely nailed what made the post divisive: the still-germinating "proper language" for describing this game development process. And that doesn't invalidate the distress of the veteran developers who've
made Bluesky
their collective watering hole.
Related:
Co-dev case study: How Blackbird Interactive and Secret Mode helped Escape the Backrooms ride the Backrooms hype wave
The reaction spotlights why we need precise communication when describing the realities of game development—because history shows that when we boil the success of a game down to the work of a few individuals, we can literally devalue developers, and potentially erode their careers.
In-groups and out-groups already devalue developers
The phrase "core team" is a slippery term, as it has no institutional definition and circles close to concepts of in-groups and out-groups that already plague game development. You could become a core team member by being friends with the company founders or going through a long and arduous job application process. You can be excluded because of your job title, your interpersonal relationships, or in the worst case, your race, gender, or sexuality.
The phrase also comes with political and financial weight. We hear often about how core teams from large studios
become the ones
who secure funding for new startups. They're often
the last ones left
after studios lay workers off in the wake of an unsuccessful game. One investor I spoke with at DICE explained that when taking pitches, he prioritizes the strength of the core team because no matter how many employees a company hires or lays off, that's the group he expects to adapt to the changes and bring a game across the finish line.
Related:
Ubisoft Montreal employees launch collective action to preserve hybrid work schedule
At best, core teams are amazing groups of colleagues who work well and have learned how to communicate with each other. At worst, they're cliques of senior and lead developers taking credit for other employees' work, sometimes shielded from the consequences of bad behavior by their close relationships with the central group. This even bleeds into the world of distributed development, where external developers are sometimes barred from speaking with members of the "core team" or even publicizing that they worked on a given game.
That dynamic is one reason why some developers (
particularly American ones
, it seems) flinch at a future built on distributed development.
When done right, the model diversifies financial risk and preserves what works about triple-A development without the need to keep everyone under one corporate entity. When done wrong, you can wind up with a game development class system, where creative direction and funding flows in limited directions, and those not lucky enough to be at the center struggle to keep doing the work they love.
This problem is obviously organizational in nature, and not easily fixed by good copyediting. But organizations begin with language, and the language we use to define our work will define the future of video game development.
How should we describe distributed development?
So how do we define the "proper language" of distributed development? Let's dig into what made this simple sentence such a point of contention:
